analysis.one_liner: Charges a fee on carbon-intensive imports and dirtier-than-average US factories, funding clean manufacturing grants.
analysis.headline: The carbon border fee bill was introduced in June 2022 and never received a hearing or vote, dying in the Senate Finance Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge a fee on imports of carbon-intensive goods — oil, gas, coal, refined petroleum, chemicals, paper, glass, cement, lime, steel, and aluminum — when those goods are produced with more emissions per ton than the average American producer in the same industry. It would also charge US factories that are dirtier than their industry's average. The fee would start at $55 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2024 and rise each year. Three quarters of the money raised would fund grants to help factories install cleaner technology, with priority for communities that lost manufacturing jobs or carry heavy pollution; the rest would fund international climate and clean energy programs. Goods from the world's least developed countries would be exempt, and exports would get their charges rebated.
analysis.who_benefits: American manufacturers whose plants are cleaner than their industry's average would avoid the domestic charge and gain a price advantage over dirtier foreign competitors. Communities near polluting factories — especially areas that lost manufacturing jobs or have high pollution burdens — would benefit from grant-funded upgrades and cleaner air. The public broadly gains from reduced emissions in the most carbon-intensive industries. The State Department's international climate programs would gain a dedicated funding stream.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cleaner US manufacturers and polluted communities

how_it_helps.text: It puts a rising price on carbon-intensive production, starting at $55 per ton in 2024 and climbing each year with inflation plus 5 percentage points, which pushes manufacturers to cut emissions or pay.

It directs 75% of the money raised into competitive grants for factories to install technology that lowers their carbon intensity, with preference for projects in communities that lost manufacturing jobs or carry high pollution burdens.
It directs the remaining 25% to State Department programs supporting climate and clean energy internationally.
It charges imports only when they are dirtier than the US industry average, so cleaner American producers gain an edge against high-polluting foreign competition.

analysis.who_pays: Importers of carbon-intensive goods would owe the charge, and much of it would reach consumers as higher prices on imported steel, cement, glass, fertilizer, and finished goods containing those materials. Domestic facilities producing more pollution per ton than their industry average would pay the fee directly. Energy-intensive manufacturers using imported inputs would face higher costs once the finished-goods charge begins.

drawbacks.text: The charge would raise the price of imported steel, cement, glass, fertilizer, and finished goods containing those materials, and importers would likely pass part of that cost to consumers.

Determining carbon intensity for foreign goods requires judging other countries' economy-wide emissions and verifying foreign factory data, an administrative task the bill leaves to Treasury and international coordination; the bill text sets detailed rules but success would depend on getting reliable data from trading partners.

Because domestic producers pay only when they are dirtier than their industry's average, the fee gives the average US plant no direct penalty and does little on its own for facilities that are merely average, not clean.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: emissions fall in some of the most polluting industries, and 75% of the money raised goes back into cleaning up plants, with priority for communities that lost manufacturing jobs and carry heavy pollution burdens. The costs are concrete: imported steel, cement, glass, fertilizer, and finished goods containing them would get more expensive, and consumers would absorb some of that. The design hedges the burden — only producers dirtier than their industry's average pay, exports are rebated, and the poorest countries are exempt — but the compliance machinery for judging foreign carbon intensity is complicated and untested. On balance it is a serious climate-and-manufacturing bill whose main drawback is higher prices for carbon-heavy goods and a heavy administrative lift.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2022, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Clean Competition Act on June 7, 2022, joined by Senators Coons, Schatz, and Heinrich.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day, and the action record shows no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The bill would have imposed a carbon intensity charge starting in 2024 on covered imports and on US facilities dirtier than their industry average, at $55 per ton in 2024, rising annually.
It would have routed 75% of the revenue into factory decarbonization grants and 25% into State Department climate programs.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers, refiners, and importers of carbon-intensive goods avoided the new charge, and the status quo on carbon-heavy trade continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Carbon-intensive producers and importers dodged the fee

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: 3 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Coons of Delaware, Schatz of Hawaii, Heinrich of New Mexico)

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties actually stood.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel extraction (oil, natural gas, coal)
industries.note: Listed as covered industries: their production would face the carbon intensity charge and imports of their products would be charged too. Their interest in killing the bill runs against the public's interest in lower emissions.
Refineries and petrochemical plants are covered and would pay if dirtier than their industry average, but US plants cleaner than the average gain protection against dirtier imports.

industries.industry: US steel, aluminum, cement, glass, and lime makers
industries.note: Low-intensity US plants gain a price edge over dirtier foreign rivals, while dirtier plants owe the charge; the industry as a whole gains a protective border against high-polluting imports, the benefit of which consumers partly give back in higher prices.
Importers would owe the charge on dirtier-than-average goods, likely passing some cost to buyers. Their loss is the point of the bill: making dirty imports reflect their emissions.

75% of the revenue funds grants for emission-cutting equipment at covered facilities, creating a market for decarbonization technology. This benefit runs alongside the public's interest in lower emissions and cleaner air.
